rules.statement: When selecting a key to sign or encrypt with, take only a key in its active window (activation passed, and neither retirement nor expiry passed), never any key just because it fits the algorithm.
rules.why: A key published ahead of its activation must not sign yet, and a retired key must stop signing while its tokens are still valid. Judging the instants on every replica's clock hands over to the successor without coordination.
rules.check: Look at credential or key selection code that filters by algorithm or key type but never checks the activation, retirement and expiry instants against the current time.

rules.statement: When several active keys fit, prefer the one that expires last, and make any caller that passes its own keys to the selector order them itself.
rules.why: The selector takes the first active key that fits, so the order of the keys decides which one is preferred.
rules.check: Look for a key collection or selector input that isn't ordered by expiry (latest first), or a selector that picks some other active key.

rules.statement: When verifying or decrypting a token, never try a key that expired more than the validation's clock skew ago, and refuse such a token as key-not-found. Keep accepting retired keys that haven't expired yet.
rules.why: A token's own lifetime is judged with clock skew, so a key's expiry must get the same tolerance. A retired key must keep serving the tokens it signed until it expires.
rules.check: Look for token validation that tries keys without checking their expiry, checks expiry without the configured clock skew, or rejects keys that are retired but not yet expired.

rules.statement: In a JSON Web Key Set, publish every key in its validity window, including keys that aren't active yet and keys that are retired, and never publish an expired key.
rules.why: Verifiers that cache the set must hold a successor key before it signs anything, and must keep a retired key until every token it signed has expired (OIDC Core §10.1.1, RFC 7517 §5).
rules.check: Look for JWKS code that publishes only active keys, or that publishes expired keys.

rules.statement: Judge a key's or credential's time windows against the clock at each use. Don't filter keys once at poll or cache time, and don't store a lifecycle state column that a background job advances.
rules.why: A key that expires between polls would stay in use for up to the poll interval, and a job that falls behind would let a key sign past its retirement. The instants are the state, and the state name is derived from them.
rules.check: Look for expiry or activation filtering done when a collection is loaded or cached, or for a persisted status field (upcoming, active, retired) that a scheduled job updates.

rules.statement: An expired credential must stop authenticating, and a certificate-backed key must expire no later than its certificate.
rules.why: An expired key must never verify, decrypt, be published or authenticate, on any path and for any owner.
rules.check: Look for client authentication that doesn't check the credential's expiry, or for keys built from certificates that don't take the certificate's NotAfter as their expiry.

rules.statement: Check the ordering of a secret's lifecycle instants (created ≤ activates ≤ retires ≤ expires) before generating or importing any key material, and answer a management request that is out of order with 400, naming the pair that is out of order.
rules.why: There is one ordering rule, and every create, import and update must apply it before any material exists.
rules.check: Look for generate, import, create or update paths that produce material or persist a secret before validating the order of its instants, or that return an error without naming the offending pair.

rules.statement: When an update omits a lifecycle instant, keep the stored value (bounded by the new expiry), and reject an update whose new expiry would make a key active again. Reactivation must be explicit.
rules.why: A retired or upcoming key must stay so unless the update names the instant. A key that resumes signing must be a deliberate act, never a side effect of extending its expiry.
rules.check: Look for update handlers that reset omitted instants to defaults, or that let an expiry change quietly reactivate a retired key.

rules.statement: Refuse a request field that the target cannot honor with a 400 instead of silently dropping it.
rules.why: Quietly ignoring an instant a secret cannot honor misleads the caller about what was stored.
rules.check: Look for request mapping that ignores fields that don't apply to the kind of resource being created, instead of returning a validation error.

rules.statement: Implement a time-window or invariant check once, and call that one implementation from every path, both stored records and runtime objects, instead of repeating the comparison in each consumer.
rules.why: A rule enforced in one place is no rule for the others, and duplicate logic lets a stored secret and its runtime key disagree.
rules.check: Look for inline comparisons of activation, retirement or expiry instants that duplicate an existing shared lifecycle helper.

rules.statement: Make a member of a persisted record that the serving code always writes required on the record, not nullable with a fallback each reader applies. Keep optional values on the request instead.
rules.why: Every reader would have to carry the fallback, and a record missing a member the serving code writes is malformed.
rules.check: Look for nullable members on a persisted data contract that readers fill in with `??` defaults.

rules.statement: Change a stored record's metadata with a `with` copy of the record, so every other member is preserved, not by building a new instance member by member.
rules.why: A `with` copy keeps every member the change doesn't name, so an update can't drop a field.
rules.check: Look for update code that builds a new record with an object initializer and copies members by hand, where a `with` expression would apply.
